newsitem.title: CHINA: China ends Communist plenum, calls for orthodoxy.
newsitem.headline: China ends Communist plenum, calls for orthodoxy.

text.p: By William Kazer
China's ruling Communist Party wound up its annual policy-making plenum on Thursday, vowing to boost orthodox socialist values that have been eroded by nearly two decades of economic reforms.
The ruling Communist Party also announced it would hold its next congress, its 15th such meeting, in late 1997.

"It should be clearly seen... in some places and departments, the problem of neglecting ideological education and cultural progress has not been solved," the Xinhua news agency quoted a plenum communique as saying.

"There are still quite a few problems, some of them quite serious in social and cultural life," the communique said. It said a top-level group would be formed to deal with those issues, which it did not identify.

The party, after four days of closed-door meetings, paid homage to paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, the architect of the market-oriented economic reforms that have helped to undermine socialist values.
State television made repeated references to the 92-year-old leader who has not been seen in public for more than two years.
But the ruling party also noted spiritual values could not be sacrificed in the name of economic reforms Deng spearheaded.
"At no time can we sacrifice spiritual values in the name of momentary economic development," the communique said.
Television showed President and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin, sporting a red tie with his grey Western business suit, as he presided over the meeting of the party's leaders.

In a display of apparent unity, television showed a sea of raised hands, against a backdrop of huge red banners flanking an oversized hammer and sickle as the communist elite voted on the final communique.

There was no announcement of personnel changes in the top echelons of the Politburo, China's most powerful decision-making body, or other party organisations. Chinese sources had said changes in top jobs were unlikely at this meeting.

Diplomats said a reshuffle was unlikely because this could upset the current delicate balance of power and alliances in the party central committee and Politburo as jockeying for position begins in the run-up to the crucial party congress next year.

"The congress is a meeting of great significance to be held at an important period during which China's reform and opening-up and socialist modernisation construction will be carried forward and forge ahead into the future," the communique said.

"It will be a historic meeting for the CPC (Communist Party of China) to lead the Chinese people... to advance, in an all-round way, the great cause of building socialism with Chinese characteristics into the new century," it said.

Jiang had been expected to seize on the plenum as the last chance before the congress to underline his role as anointed heir to Deng Xiaoping, who has been fading gradually from the scene, diplomats and Chinese sources said.
Deng's economic reforms have eroded what Beijing's top leaders regard as orthodox Marxist values, and party chief Jiang has made clear he wants to place his stamp on ideology in China.
The party mouthpiece, the People's Daily, has filled its front page for several days with examples of model workers whose socialist values the populace at large should strive to emulate.

Among these was Beijing bus conductress Li Shuli, who is said to rise at 4 a.m. to make sure she is familiar with major sites along the route so she can help disoriented passengers. She then washes the bus windows.
Diplomats said Jiang was using the campaign -- coupled with a tough line on the media and ideology -- to boost his position.
